
Of all canton-specific provisions in @tbl-counterfactual-rules several do not affect the smaller-party outcomes. For example, were the statutory tie-breaking rules in Schaffhausen, Uri, and Zurich not triggered in any analyzed election. The Schaffhausen rule for calculating the distribution number though, produced differences in two cases: 5,022 rather than 5,023 in Klettgau in 2008 and 2,196 rather than 2,197 in Neuhausen in 2024. These differences changed neither the initial nor the final seat allocation. In Schwyz 2024 and in Graubünden 2022, an unresolved exact tie produced alternative HB allocations for parties above the 10% threshold. Thus it only affected individual party totals but not the aggregated seat total of smaller parties used in the main analysis. The relative-majority allocation in Schaffhausen’s single-seat district was nevertheless applied and remains part of the reconstructed fomrmer system. ^[These findings are based on the author’s calculations of the official election data described in Appendix 1. Sources for the applicable legal provisions are provided in the preceding footnote.]

Beyond the statutory allocation rules, the counterfactual requires an assumption about unobserved list alliances. Unlike Leuzinger and Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, this analysis does not carry historical or hypothetical alliances forward. List alliances are in this thesis seen as strategic and election-specific rather than fixed institutional parameters. This leads to, that election-specific, historical alliances cannot simply be assumed to persist across subsequent elections with different parties and vote distributions. In Zurich, for example, the last Kantonsrat election under Hagenbach–Bischoff took place in 2003. Assuming that the alliances formed in 2003 would still have applied in 2023 despite two decades of changes in the party system would therefore introduce a strong and unverifiable behavioural assumption. Some parties that formed list alliances in Zurich in 2003 no longer existed or contested the 2023 election. Conversely, parties such as the Green Liberal Party, which contested the 2023 election, did not yet exist in 2003. (Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2003, table 3; Statistisches Amt des Kantons Zürich 2026; Grünliberale Partei Kanton Zürich n.d.). Therefore the counterfactual preserves joint lists or list groups represented as a single unit in the observed election data. But it does not reconstruct historical alliances or assume new alliances between separately reported units. This provides a transparent counterfactual that holds the observed electoral configuration constant and estimates the mechanical allocation difference between the specified election-specific regimes.

The exclusion of unobserved list alliances is an important limitation of the counterfactual. Under Hagenbach–Bischoff, list alliances can pool votes during seat allocation and thereby improve the chances of representation for smaller lists (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590). If the parties observed under Double Pukelsheim would have formed such alliances under the counterfactual HB regime, excluding them may understate smaller parties’ counterfactual HB seat totals and consequently overstate their estimated gain under Double Pukelsheim. However, neither the composition of these hypothetical alliances nor the distribution of any resulting seat gains can be reliably determined. Alliance gains could accrue to larger partners or leave the aggregated representation of parties below the 10% threshold unchanged. The direction is therefore theoretically plausible but cannot be quantified uniformly across elections.

A second research-design choice concerns the electoral units and their seat magnitudes. In most cantons, the reform retained the former territorial districts or municipalities, meaning that the observed electoral units broadly correspond to those previously used under HB. The principal scope deviations are addressed in the special-cases callout below. Regarding the district magnitudes, the use of election-specific magnitudes is deliberate. District seat entitlements are generally based on population and periodically recalculated. Consequently, the magnitudes from the last pre-reform election would not necessarily have remained applicable in later elections even if Hagenbach–Bischoff had been retained. The counterfactual therefore holds each observed election’s electoral units and seat magnitudes constant across the two regimes. It asks how the same votes would have been translated into seats under the former district-level rules, conditional on the contemporary distribution of seats among districts. 

The remaining deviations from this general approach are summarized below.

::: {.callout-note title="Treatment of the Special Cases"}
**Graubünden.** The HB allocation is hypothetical and applied using the common allocation procedure employed elsewhere in the analysis. It's basic formula is taken from the former Aargau Law (Kanton Aargau, 1988/2004, § 12 and § 13(1)(a–b)). Thus the observations are shown in grey and excluded from the main transition estimate. In the 2022 election, appears an unresolved exact tie between the "FDP" and "SP_GRUENE" in Rheinwald, to resolve it an hypothetical lot would be needed. The tie, which doesn't affect the aggregated seat total of smaller parties, is therefore retained as an unresolved amlternative in the counterfactual.(Kanton Aargau, 2004, § 13; author’s calculations using Kanton Graubünden, 2022) Robustness checks using Zurich’s party-vote tie-breaker and Schaffhausen’s ceiling-based quota preserved all possible allocations across the 39 districts in both 2022 and 2026 (Kanton Zürich, 1983/2005, § 88b; Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 1979, § 36).

**Zug.** Neuheim used Majorz before the reform. An exact Majorz counterfactual cannot be reconstructed because the results of a hypothetical second ballot are unobservable. Neuheim is therefore included using a hypothetical HB allocation.(BGE 136 I 376 E. 5.1; Kanton Zug, 2022a, 2022b, 2022c, 2026) The specific implementation approach adopted for Neuheim has no bearing on the main analysis.

**Uri.** Only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf used Double Pukelsheim in the elections analyzed here. They account for 37 of the Landrat's 64 seats (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2020, p. 1). Uri's vote shares, including the less-than-10% classification of smaller parties, are therefore based only on the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim, not on the whole canton.

**Valais.** Unlike in the other cantons, upper apportionment is conducted separately within six electoral regions rather than canton-wide. Seats and votes are aggregated at the cantonal level only for this analysis; the actual allocation occurs independently within each region (Lüscher, 2024, p. 57).

**Schaffhausen.** The parliament was reduced from 80 to 60 seats when Double Pukelsheim was introduced. The counterfactual retains the 60-seat structure because comparing the two allocation methods requires the same number and distribution of seats (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, pp. 1-2, 6).
:::

With the counterfactual rules and scope established, the next subsection describes the official election data and their standardization across cantons.

### Data Sources and Processing {#sec-data-cleaning}

This subsection describes the official election data used in the analysis and explains how the heterogeneous cantonal source files were transformed into a harmonized dataset.

The official election results were obtained primarily from publicly available datasets published by cantonal state chancelleries and statistical offices. Where the data wasn't available online in structured formats, such as CSV or XLSX, they were requested from the responsible cantonal authorities directly. All contacted authorities except the Canton of Schaffhausen provided data in either CSV or XLSX.  Therrefore the Schaffhausen results had to be extracted from official PDF documents. The precise sources and elections covered are reported in Appendix `#ref(<tbl-data-sources>)`{=typst}. The granularity and organization of the source data vary considerably across cantons and elections, ranging from canton-wide files to separate district- or municipality-level results. In Schwyz, for example, the 2016 results were distributed across 30 municipality-specific excel workbooks, whereas the 2020 and 2024 results were each provided in a single workbook. Further did the structure of the files differ, some such as the Graubünden ones, were prepared for public or media use and through that readily accessible, while others had originally been designed for internal administrative calculations and where therefore less structured. 

Party and list names were standardized using readable, clear and consistent abbreviations. The same political organization was assigned a common identifier across cantons and elections, some of the examples include "SVP", "GLP", "ALG", and "PIRATEN". Meaningful changes over time were nevertheless retained. In particular, "CVP" and "BDP" remain separately identified before their merger, while "DIEMITTE" is used only after the formation of the new party in 2021 (H.-P. Schaub, 2022). In bilingual Valais, French- and German-language labels referring to the same party were harmonized, generally using the German abbreviation for consistency with the other cantons. However, "SP_GAUCHE_CITOYENNE" and "SP_GRUENE_UNABHAENGIGE" were retained as distinct identifiers because they represented separately reported lists with partly different organizations in the background.

The treatment of joint and affiliated lists follows the electoral units reported in the official results. Where several political organizations contested an election on a single joint list, that list was treated as one analytical unit. Examples include "SP_GRUENE" in Graubünden in 2022 and "FGA_AL_PDA" in Zurich in 2023. It's important to state that joint lists and list alliances used under Hagenbach-Bischoff differ fundamentally. When forming a joint list, parties run together as a single electoral list (party), while under list alliances the parties run separately and the votes of the alliance parties are pooled later for the seat-allocation. (Pukelsheim & Schuhmacher, 2011, p. 1590) In addition to joint lists, in some cantons also affiliated or special-interest lists ran as a independent list. This phenomena occurred especially strong in Schaffhausen were among others the following affiliated lists ran for the 2016 election : "SVP_KMU" (SVP's small and medium enterprises list),"SVP_SEN" (SVP's senior's list), "JUSO" (Young Socialists) and "JFSH" (Young Liberals) (Kanton Schaffhausen, n.d.). Since these lists entered the official Double Pukelsheim allocation separately, they were also retained as separate units in the analysis. The analysis therefore contains exactly the lists which ran in the corresponding election with the effect that this decision possibly affects the measured number and seat share of smaller parties.

Beyond the harmonization of party and list names, the cleaning process involved restructuring vote data, identifying the relevant electoral units, and assigning their election-specific seat totals. The source files were converted into comparable tables containing party votes and the seat magnitude of each electoral district. Where parties appeared in separate columns, as in Aargau, Graubünden, and Nidwalden, these columns were reshaped into the variables *parties* and *party_votes*. Candidate-level exports required a different treatment. In all four Zug and Schwyz’s 2020 election, each candidate row repeated the corresponding list’s vote and seat totals. The scripts first checked that these repeated values were consistent and then retained one observation per municipality and list, preventing the totals from being counted multiple times. Source variables such as *list_votes* and *election_mandates* were thereby converted into *party_votes* and *district_seats*.
The geographic preparation depended on the structure of the official files. In Zurich, municipal party votes were summed within the electoral districts identified by the source variable *Geschaeft*. Aargau’s files already contained district totals, which were selected using the *DISTRICT* classification. Similarly, the Graubünden script extracted the existing district totals by carrying each *Wahlkreis* heading down to its corresponding *Total* row. Municipalities were retained as allocation units in Nidwalden, Schwyz, and Zug. Their names were extracted from the source tables or, for Schwyz in 2016, from the municipality-specific filenames. Uri’s script explicitly selected the workbook blocks for Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf. In Valais, the 14 districts were assigned to six electoral regions in R according to the official electoral structure, preserving the different geographic levels required for the district-level HB counterfactual and the regional DP upper apportionment.

District seat magnitudes were obtained from the available official information for each election. In Aargau, district names were matched to officially sourced seat vectors or separate seat-allocation tables provided by the canton officials. Valais used explicitly recorded district magnitudes for each election year. In Zurich and Graubünden, magnitudes were reconstructed by counting elected candidates within each district. In Uri and Schwyz’s 2016 election, they were calculated by summing the official DP seats within each municipality.

The shared finalization function then produced one observation per standardized party or list code and election. It created an election identifier combining the canton abbreviation and election year, such as *ZH_23*, and joined the HB and DP seat totals by party. The final columns were *election_id*, *parties*, *vote_share*, *small_party*, *seats_hb*, *seats_dp*, *parliament_size*, and *seats_allocated_dp*. The last two variables distinguish the full parliament from the seats covered by the comparison, this because of the Canton Uri, where these values are 64 and 37, respectively. District identifiers, raw party votes, and district magnitudes served as intermediate inputs rather than columns in the final combined dataset.

Vote shares were derived using the information available in each canton’s official election files. In Aargau, Zurich, Zug, and Valais, party votes were divided by the corresponding district’s seat magnitude to obtain voter equivalents. These quotients were rounded to the nearest integer, with half values rounded upwards, before being summed by party across districts. Each party’s vote share was then calculated as its aggregated voter number divided by the total voter number of all included parties, multiplied by 100. Nidwalden instead used the voter numbers supplied in the official upper-apportionment worksheet. Schaffhausen used the published voter numbers extracted from the official result PDFs. Further where there the reconstructed voter numbers compared with the published values using election-specific tolerances to accommodate differences in reporting precision. Other datasets supplied vote shares directly or required different denominators. In Schwyz, the 2016 shares were calculated from each party’s total cantonal votes relative to the sum of votes for all retained party lists, excluding the category for ballots without a party designation. For 2020, the denominator was the total accounted votes, counted once per municipality and checked against the summed list votes. The 2024 Schwyz shares and the Graubünden shares were taken directly from the official cantonal summaries. Uri’s published shares refer exclusively to the four relevant municpialites and could therefore be retained. The shared finalization function rounded all vote shares to four decimal places.

The Double Pukelsheim results were assembled separately within the canton-specific scripts from official seat tables, municipal allocations, or elected-candidate records. Valais required a separate reconstruction of the upper apportionment within its six electoral regions, followed by comparisons with published official results. Each script supplied its election-specific DP results to the shared finalization function, which joined them to the HB counterfactuals by standardized party identifier. Validation routines checked electoral-unit coverage and seat totals and, where alternative representations were available, reconciled candidate counts or aggregated lower allocations with reported list mandates or upper-apportionment totals. District-level consistency checks and final allocation totals were applied according to the available source structure. Uri’s allocation checks covered the 37 proportional seats included in the analysis, while the full parliamentary size remained recorded as 64. Unresolved HB ties were retained as alternative allocations.

One of the consistency checks revealed an error in the Zurich 2011 election data. There the party-votes total for the Socialdemocrats, were dobuled across all constituencies. The mistakes was found through the comparison of the summed party votes with the reported unit totals and cross-checking candidate and supplementary votes. Followingly, the error was reported to the Statistical Office of the Canton of Zurich. They confirmed the mistake and resolved it, the underlying cause was that a duplicate SP entry in the list-to-party mapping table had caused double counting during the aggregation of the official municipal results. The corrected dataset was uploaded and is used in this analysis. (S.Graf, personal communication, 2026-09-11)

All processing was implemented in the canton-specific R scripts in *data_cleaning_cantons*, supported by the shared functions in *00_functions.R*. Each *process_canton_*()* function combined its cleaned elections into a cantonal dataset. These nine datasets were subsequently appended row-wise using *bind_rows()* to create *all_elections*, preserving one observation per standardized party or list and election. Detailed procedures, source-specific exceptions, and validation arrangements are documented in Appendix 1, with the cleaning code provided in Appendix 2.

### Measures and Analytical Strategy {#sec-measures}

The *analyzed_area* comprises the whole canton except in Uri, where it covers only Altdorf, Bürglen, Erstfeld, and Schattdorf, the four municipalities using Double Pukelsheim. These municipalities account for 37 of the canton's 64 parliamentary seats. The variable *seats_allocated_dp* records the number of seats covered by the comparison, while *parliament_size* records the full size of the cantonal parliament. These values are equal in all analyzed cantons except Uri.

For the purposes of this thesis, a smaller party is defined as an electoral list or list group with a vote share below 10% in the analyzed area. Youth lists and other affiliated lists are treated as separate analytical units whenever they enter the official Double Pukelsheim allocation separately. Accordingly, the term *party* refers to the standardized electoral list or list group recorded in the dataset and does not necessarily correspond to a broader organizational party family. *Smaller parties* are identified separately for each election using their observed vote shares. The same set of smaller parties is then used when comparing the two seat allocations within that election.

The main analysis compares the combined seat shares of smaller parties within each election. For this purpose, the seats of all lists below the 10% vote-share threshold are summed separately under Double Pukelsheim and Hagenbach–Bischoff. Each total is divided by the number of analyzed seats, recorded in *seats_allocated_dp*, and multiplied by 100 to obtain the corresponding seat share as a percentage. This produces one aggregate seat-share difference per election. Using *seats_allocated_dp* as the denominator ensures that the measure refers to the same area as the votes and seat allocations included in the comparison.

The election-level outcome is the difference between these two seat shares, denoted by $\Delta_e$ and defined in Hypothesis 1. Positive values indicate that smaller parties collectively receive a larger seat share under Double Pukelsheim while negative values indicate a smaller share. A value of five percentage points therefore means that their combined share of the analyzed seats is five percentage points higher under Double Pukelsheim. This also means, that a negative or positive aggregate difference, does not mean that each included party gains or loses seats respectively. 

Hypothesis 1 is assessed using the average seat-share differnce aross all 31 elections. In that analysis every elections receives equal weight, which means that cantons with more elections held under DP are influencing the average stronger. Since the parliament sizes differ, a supplementary weighted mean is added, where elections with a bigger parliament influence the mean stronger. It expresses the total net seat gain of smaller parties across the included elections as a percentage of the total analyzed seats, giving greater weight to elections with more seats. To better display the variation and typical gain, the median ,the first and third quartiles are reported additionally. The main summaries exclude Graubünden for the reasons set out in @sec-assumptions-scope its observations are presented separately for context.

All four exploratory analyses are descriptive. They examine differences across institutional settings and successive elections without isolating the causal effects of individual electoral rules.

For EQ1, election-level seat-share gains are first averaged within each canton. These canton-level outcomes are examined against mean district magnitude, median district magnitude, the share of districts below nine seats, and CV.  These measure are all calculated from the same fixed allocation in each canton's last pre-reform election and the Schaffhausen parliament adjusted to 60 seats. These historical characteristics are held fixed when comparing the canton-level average gains across the analyzed elections. Uri covers the same four municipalities included in the HB–DP comparison, and Valais's district count refers to its 14 Hagenbach-Bischoff allocation districts. CV divides the population standard deviation of the baseline district magnitudes by their baseline mean. A higher CV indicates greater dispersion relative to average district size. All district measures are calculated once per canton from this baseline and are held fixed across its analyzed elections. For each measure, cantons are grouped below or at or above its unweighted mean across the eight transition cantons. Group means give each canton equal weight, and the group difference is calculated as below-mean minus at-or-above-mean. Graubünden is shown only for context and excluded from cutoffs and group means.

The historical reference year applies to all district measures. Historical seat allocations are documented in the cantonal publications and court judgments cited below.^[Sources by canton and reference year: Aargau 2005 (Kanton Aargau, 2004); Graubünden 2018 (Kanton Graubünden, n.d.); Nidwalden 2010 (BGE 136 I 352, E. 3.5); Schaffhausen 2004, adjusted to 60 seats (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, Table 1, p. 2); Schwyz 2012 (Urteil des Bundesgerichts 1C_407/2011 vom 19. März 2012, Sachverhalt A); Uri 2016 (Standeskanzlei Uri, 2016, p. 5); Valais 2013 (BGE 140 I 107, Sachverhalt A); Zug 2010 (Staatskanzlei des Kantons Zug, 2010, p. 92); Zurich 2003 (Regierungsrat des Kantons Zürich, 2002).] Later district magnitudes may change, so the district measures describe associations with the initial structure. For Schaffhausen, the 2004 structure is adjusted from 80 to 60 seats using the published hypotethical allocation in the government's reform report (Regierungsrat des Kantons Schaffhausen, 2007, Table 1, p. 2). The election-specific Hagebach-Bischoff to Double Pukelsheim allocations are unchanged.

For the comparison by Double Pukelsheim seat count, election-level differences are first averaged within each canton. Cantons are then grouped according to whether they allocate atleast 100 or fewer than 100 seats through Double Pukelsheim. The 100-seat cutoff serves as a descriptive grouping of the observed cantons. Group means are calculated from the canton-level averages, giving each canton equal weight irrespective of the number of observed elections. The difference between the group means is calculated as the mean for cantons with atleast 100 seats minus the mean for cantons with fewer than 100 seats. Graubünden is excluded from these group means. Given the small number of cantons and their differing electoral rules, the comparison is interpreted descriptively.

For EQ3, elections are grouped by whether or not an explicit electoral quorum applied under Double Pukelsheim. Within each group, the mean of $\Delta_e$ gives each election equal weight, so cantons with more observed elections contribute more. The group difference is calculated as the mean without a quorum minus the mean with one. Graubünden is shown for context and excluded from both means. Since the observations differ structurally in terms of quorum levels, geographical scope and others, the analysis is only descriptive.

To examine successive elections, the seat-share difference $\Delta_e$ is plotted separately for each canton and its successive elections. The aim is to analyze whether the mechanical seat-share gain persists across elections. To identify possible influencing factors, they are noted next to the election in which they ocurred. Later changes and fluctuations are interpreted with the help of the additional context provided by the notes. Besides the separate analyis of each canton, the results are also set into the between-canton context to possibly identify general patterns.
